title: Pip's Crag Caper
markdown:
High country: hills like green steps, cedar forests, villages tucked under cliffs. In one of them lived Tansy, who was not a cackling wart-nosed sort of witch. Quietly practical, a twinkle, a smudge of soot that seemed permanent on her cheek. Her cottage overflowed with dried herbs, cinnamon, lavender. Sunlight found dusty spellbooks and a hearth that stayed warm.

Bramble the hedgehog was fiercely loyal, snuffles and sharp chirps that Tansy understood. He knew when she needed a prickly warmth at her feet. The real heart of the house, and a great deal of her magic, was Pip: a griffin chick, not the eagle-headed beasts of legend but a fluffball of down, clumsy paws, stubby wings that fluttered without asking, an appetite for sunbeams and naps. He chose impossible places to slumber, and Tansy’s heart leapt every time.

One crisp morning smelled of roasting nuts and mountain air: the Whispering Wind Festival in Stonehaven. Saffron and sky-blue banners on impossibly high poles. Tansy, Bramble, and Pip on their way, Pip in a wool-lined basket. Then a playful gust, banners wild, a moment adjusting a shawl—and Pip was gone.

“Pip!” Calm voice, urgent eyes. Bramble hopped from the satchel, nose twitching. Not in the basket, not at her feet, not in the cloak. Festival noise suddenly too loud.

Pip’s naps were legendary. Last week: dusty rafters of the blacksmith’s forge. The week before: a hollowed pumpkin at market, a delighted squeak on waking. Tansy searched, Bramble trotting with the determination of a very small general. Cliffside stalls, textiles, spices, a man selling roasted nuts who had not seen a griffin and would have remembered. “A fluffy bumbling chick, about this big?” Hands measured the air. Heads shook, busy with wares, though one child pointed helpfully at a pigeon, which was the wrong species and knew it.

They found Cricket weaving through with surprising speed: a goblin, pebble-eyes, a knowledge of the mountains that was frankly astonishing, a quiet observer. “Pip?” A rumble like stones underground. “The small one. High, quiet places. Especially near the Old Crag. He likes the way the wind whispers there.”

The Old Crag: sheer face, wobbly ledges, rare plants. Home also to Old Man Hemlock, creature of ritual, believer in the traditions that held the mountain together. His current ritual baffled everyone. The festival could only begin, he insisted, once a specific offering of gratitude sat on the highest altar overlooking the valley. The problem: nobody, not even Hemlock, quite remembered what the offering was, or where to find it.

“Whisperwind Moss,” Hemlock declared, raspy, convicted. “A very specific moss. One place, high on the Crag. For the ancestors. Vital for the year’s blessings.” Villagers shuffled. The Crag was steep. Nobody was eager to climb it on a whim.

Tansy observed: worried glances, Hemlock’s genuine conviction even with fuzzy details. Bramble sniffed a damp patch near the altar, nudged an almost invisible clump, looked up with an insistent chirp. “Whisperwind Moss,” Tansy murmured. “Pip loves the smell. Reminds him of his first sunbeam, when it grew wild near the cottage.”

She looked up the cliff. A tiny fluffy shape on a ledge, fast asleep, silhouette against blue. Pip. Ultimate nap: highest, quietest. And clinging to the same ledge, just within a sleeping griffin’s reach, a lush patch of vibrant green Whisperwind Moss.

“The offering.” A slow knowing smile. “Not for the ancestors, Cricket. For Pip. Hemlock’s memory is mixing things.” Sparkle of a plan. “Can you get that moss?”

Cricket, nimble, a rope that seemed to appear from nowhere, scrambled like a shadow. He gathered a small bundle, earthy and sweet, stone and sky. Descending, he held it aloft, a green triumph.

“Pip!” Tansy’s voice on the wind. “Smells good. Come down, little one.”

Fluffy head stirred. Enormous golden eyes, heavy with sleep. Moss. Tansy below, arms open. Bramble, little tail of relief. A happy clumsy flutter, a tumble of down and joy, a soft thud in Tansy’s arms.

He snuggled, chirped, nuzzled her cheek. Safe. The crowd, which had been pretending not to watch a witch rescue a nap, made the small warm noise crowds make when they are relieved. Hemlock, peering at the moss Cricket had brought, decided it would do for the altar after all, which was convenient, since the chick had already chosen the true high place. He placed it with the gravity of a man who had always meant this. The banners went on dancing. Pip, most inconveniently napping griffin in the high country, went back in the basket and, for the length of one hymn, actually stayed. Bramble chirped once, which Tansy took as: we are not doing the rafters again this week.
characters: Tansy (quietly practical witch), Bramble (a fiercely loyal hedgehog), Cricket (a goblin who knows the mountains)
audience: children aged 9-10, amusing fantasy story for middle-grade readers
